title: The examination as an instrument
description: How to run the neurologic examination as a series of experiments on circuits, from watching a child before touching them and turning tests into play to reading the infant reflexes that are meant to come and go.
why: Done well, the neurologic examination is a series of small experiments, each one testing whether a particular circuit works.
objectives: Explain each part of the examination as a test of a circuit, and record observations before interpretations.
Collect most of a child's examination by observation before touching.
Adapt the examination to newborns, infants, toddlers, school-age children and adolescents.
Order a toddler examination so that cooperation lasts, and avoid the common technical errors.
Use the primitive reflexes and postural reactions to detect upper motor neuron dysfunction in infancy.
Read each infant finding as a pair of finding and age, and explain why age is a coordinate of localization.

sections.title: What the examination is for
sections.content:
To an onlooker, a neurologic examination can look like a ritual, with the same hammer taps, the same light shone in the eyes and the same request to touch your nose. Performed as a ritual it is slow and nearly useless. Performed well, **each maneuver is a small experiment that tests whether a particular circuit is intact.**

The idea fits in two words, **think circuitry**, and it comes with a procedure (DeMyer, p. 36). First you record what you actually observed, in plain terms. Only then do you translate it into what it means about the nervous system. Weakness and brisk reflexes on one side, for example, become a hemiplegia from interruption of the pyramidal tract, which places the lesion in a circuit (DeMyer, p. 36). A conclusion written without its observation can't be checked, either by the next examiner or by you when the picture changes.

There are three standards for deciding whether something is abnormal. You compare it with the norm for a person of the same age and sex, with its mate on the other side, and with the family (DeMyer, p. 36). The third is the easiest to forget and is especially useful in children. A large head in a child whose father also has a large head is often a harmless family trait, while a wide-based gait that matches a parent's points toward an inherited cause.

**Screening and targeting**

Nobody performs every test on every patient. An efficient neurologic examination chooses the parts that bear on the problem the history has uncovered (Morris 2012, p. xxv). A brief screening examination is done for everyone and then expanded or trimmed to fit the history, and the better the history, the briefer the examination needs to be (DeMyer, p. 604). The screen asks whether anything is wrong, and the targeted examination asks exactly where.

**Recording the examination**

"Neuro exam WNL" will not do as a note (DeMyer, p. 604). Those three letters record a verdict and leave out the evidence for it. A useful note says what you tested and what you found, especially the normal findings that bear on the question at hand. A line such as "walks, runs and hops on each foot; reflexes symmetric; toes down" tells the next reader far more.
keyPoints: Treat each part of the examination as an experiment on a circuit, which is what thinking in circuitry means (DeMyer, p. 36).
Record the observation first and the interpretation second.
Judge abnormality against age norms, against the other side and against the family (DeMyer, p. 36).
Screen everyone, then target the examination to the hypothesis the history raises (Morris 2012, p. xxv; DeMyer, p. 604).
Never write 'WNL', and record instead what was tested and what was found (DeMyer, p. 604).

question.question: A 6-year-old is seen for a large head noticed by the school nurse. Development and examination are otherwise normal. Which single extra step is most likely to change your interpretation?
options: Measuring the parents' head circumferences
Testing smell with coffee grounds
Checking the jaw jerk
Testing two-point discrimination on the fingertips
question.explanation: The third standard for judging abnormality is comparison with the family (DeMyer, p. 36). In a well child with a normal examination and a large-headed parent, a large head is often familial, so measuring the parents speaks directly to the question. Smell, the jaw jerk and two-point discrimination are legitimate tests, but none bears on the problem the history raised.

sections.title: Watching before touching
sections.content:
The most underused instrument in the pediatric neurologic examination is the examiner's patience, because **most of the examination can be done without touching the child**. Before you reach for a hammer, you can see whether the child is alert and engaged, whether both sides of the body move equally, and how each hand is used. You can also see whether the face moves symmetrically during a smile or a cry, whether there are extra movements, and how the child sits, stands, walks and plays.

Watching first is good practice with every patient, since unobtrusive observation of how someone sits, stands, walks and gestures often reveals more than formal tests, particularly in infants (DeMyer, p. 239). With a child the reason is also practical. Formal testing needs cooperation, and a young child's cooperation soon runs out. Every finding you collect by watching is one you won't have to wring from a frightened toddler later.

**What to watch for**

Watch the child for five things as you take the history from the parents.

- **Arousal and interaction.** Whether the child looks at you, tracks you, responds to voices and plays purposefully for the age.
- **Symmetry.** One arm that moves less, one hand kept fisted, a face that droops on one side.
- **Posture and tone at rest.** A frog-legged posture in an infant, a head that lags, a child who props on a wall to stand.
- **Gait and play.** Walking to the room, climbing onto a chair, picking up a toy from the floor.
- **Extra movements.** Tremor, chorea, tics, staring spells.

**Undressing the child**

It is tempting to skip undressing out of politeness, but if a third of the body stays covered, you can only do two thirds of the examination (DeMyer, p. 239). For a child that means undressing down to the underwear, with a parent present, so that you can see the back, the spine, the calves and the skin. Café-au-lait spots, a tuft of hair over the lower spine, wasted or enlarged calves, and a difference in size between the limbs of the two sides are all easy to miss through clothing.
keyPoints: Much of the pediatric examination is hands-off and can be done by watching while you take the history.
Observation of spontaneous activity often reveals more than formal tests, especially in infants (DeMyer, p. 239).
Cooperation is a limited resource, so collect what you can by watching before you touch.
Watch for arousal, symmetry, posture, gait, play and extra movements.
Undress the child, with a parent present, because a covered third of the body is an unexamined third (DeMyer, p. 239).

question.question: A 2-year-old screams as soon as you walk toward him and buries his face in his mother's shoulder. You have 20 minutes. What is the best way to begin the neurologic examination?
options: Hold him firmly and test reflexes quickly before he becomes more upset
Postpone the examination to another day
Ask his mother to describe what he can do, and rely on that instead of an examination
Sit at a distance, take the history, and watch him play, walk and use his hands before approaching
question.explanation: Sitting at a distance while you take the history lets you assess arousal, symmetry, gait and hand use without spending his cooperation, and unobtrusive observation often reveals more than formal tests (DeMyer, p. 239). Holding a frightened child down produces crying and unreliable findings. Postponing gives up information you could collect now, and his mother's report cannot replace seeing him move.

sections.title: The examination as a game, from newborn to adolescent
sections.content:
Ask a school-age child to push against your hand and you may get a polite nudge. Tell her "don't let me win," and you are far more likely to see what she can really do. Turning tests into a **friendly contest** works even with adults, and doubly well with children. Ask whether the patient can see out to the side as far as you can, or how light a touch they can feel. Challenges like these draw out the patient's best performance and keep the examiner interested too (DeMyer, p. 38). It also helps to **expect the abnormal**, because a mind that expects normal findings stops looking carefully (DeMyer, p. 38). The form the game takes changes as the child grows.

**Newborn.** Examine between feeds. Interrupting a feed produces a crying baby, and a full stomach produces a sleepy one. Watch spontaneous movements, posture and alertness before you handle the baby at all.

**Infant.** Faces, voices and bright objects test vision, hearing and eye movements, while pull to sit, ventral suspension and supported standing test tone and strength. The reflexes that should come and go are covered in section 5.

**Toddler.** At this age everything is play. A toy to follow tests eye movements, blowing a kiss and showing teeth test the face, and stacking blocks or picking up small objects tests fine motor skill and hand preference. To screen gait, ask the child to run a short distance to fetch something (Brazis 2011, p. 17). Videos of these tasks at each age are on the [Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/18month.html) site.

**School-age child.** Most formal tests become possible once they are framed as challenges, such as hopping on one foot, walking heel to toe like a tightrope walker, or "push me away". Children will refuse pinprick, but those as young as 3 will play "the temperature game" with a cool object instead (DeMyer, p. 617).

**Adolescent.** The examination is close to an adult's, with more attention to privacy and to asking the teenager alone about symptoms they may not raise in front of a parent.

**Try the figure above**, which asks you to put eight steps of a toddler examination in order. Any order within a tier counts as correct. It checks that you watch first, then play, then move to hands-on testing, and leave the things a toddler hates until last.
keyPoints: Turning tests into games and contests draws out a child's best performance (DeMyer, p. 38).
Expect the abnormal, because a mind that expects normality stops looking (DeMyer, p. 38).
Examine a newborn between feeds, a toddler through play and a school-age child through challenges.
To screen gait, have a child run a short distance to fetch something (Brazis 2011, p. 17).
Children as young as 3 will play the temperature game in place of pinprick (DeMyer, p. 617).

question.question: You need to test sensation in a 4-year-old with possible numbness of one leg. She cried when her vaccinations were given last week. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Use a safety pin on each dermatome and ask whether it feels sharp
Use the temperature game, touching each leg with a cool object and asking which feels colder, and watch her face as well as her answers
Skip sensory testing, because 4-year-olds cannot report sensation
Test vibration with a tuning fork on the toes first, because it is the most sensitive test
question.explanation: Children as young as 3 will play the temperature game (DeMyer, p. 617). It tests the same spinothalamic pathway as pinprick without making her an unwilling subject, and her face checks her answers. A pin in a child who fears needles will end the examination. Skipping sensation throws away a testable finding, and vibration tests the dorsal columns, a different pathway.

sections.title: Order and technique in the hands-on examination
sections.content:
A toddler who has cheerfully stacked blocks for ten minutes can be lost for the rest of the visit the moment a bright light comes close to his face. So **do the hands-off parts first, the games next, the hands-on parts after that, and the things a child hates last**. A tape measure round the head, a bright ophthalmoscope light and a tongue depressor can each end cooperation, so they wait until everything else is done. Reflexes are best done late, with the child on a parent's lap. Turning the reflex hammer into an imaginary horse with sound effects stops it from looking like a weapon ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/12month.html)).

**Swinging the hammer**

The commonest student error is hammer pecking, which means gripping the handle tightly and jabbing at the tendon with no wrist action. Hold the handle loosely between thumb and finger and let the hammer swing like a pendulum (DeMyer, p. 252). A reflex that seems absent after a peck is often present after a swing.

**Before you call a reflex absent**

Reposition the limb to change the tension on the tendon, or adjust the pressure of your thumb. Use **reinforcement**, for instance by asking the patient to lock their fingers together and pull hard while you tap (DeMyer, p. 258). In infants the biceps tendon can be hard to find, and the knee jerk is easiest to elicit with the leg nearly straight (DeMyer, p. 258). A child who is tense, cold or frightened will often show reflexes once relaxed.

**Testing tone**

Tone is the slight resistance you feel when you move a relaxed joint (DeMyer, p. 270). A child who "helps" you move the limb, or who stiffens in fear, will feel stiff for reasons that have nothing to do with the nervous system. Distract the child, wait, and then move the limb both slowly and quickly.

**The plantar response in a ticklish child**

Stroking the sole of a ticklish child produces a withdrawal that can look like an upgoing toe. Ticklish young patients tolerate stimulation on the lateral side of the foot better, so start there (DeMyer, p. 616).

Throughout, keep comparing one side with the other and the child with the family (DeMyer, p. 36). An asymmetry usually tells you more than any single absolute value.
keyPoints: Order the examination by tier, watching first, then playing, then hands-on testing, with the unpleasant parts last.
Do the reflexes late, on a parent's lap, with the hammer turned into a toy (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Swing the hammer loosely, since pecking is the commonest error (DeMyer, p. 252).
Before calling a reflex absent, reposition the limb, adjust your thumb and use reinforcement (DeMyer, p. 258).
Judge tone only in a relaxed limb, and in a ticklish child stroke the lateral side of the foot (DeMyer, pp. 270, 616).

question.question: A tense, anxious 6-year-old has no knee jerks on either side when you tap with the hammer gripped firmly. Strength, gait and sensation are normal. What should you do before recording areflexia?
options: Record the reflexes as absent; a normal child always has knee jerks
Order nerve conduction studies
Re-test with a loose, swinging hammer, reposition the legs, and use reinforcement such as pulling the locked fingers apart
Test the ankle jerks instead and record the knees as untestable
question.explanation: Pecking with a tight grip is the commonest technical error. Before calling a reflex absent, swing the hammer properly, reposition the limb and use reinforcement (DeMyer, pp. 252, 258). In a tense child with an otherwise normal examination, these steps usually bring the reflexes out. Recording areflexia or ordering nerve studies now risks a workup for a technical artifact.

sections.title: The infant exam: reflexes that should come and go
sections.content:
An infant's examination includes findings that are supposed to **disappear** and others that are supposed to **appear**, each on its own schedule. That schedule is a powerful localizing tool in early childhood.

**Primitive reflexes** such as the Moro, the palmar grasp and the Galant are normally present in the term newborn and diminish over the next 4 to 6 months. **Postural reactions** such as the Landau, lateral propping and the parachute emerge between about 3 and 8 months. Persistent primitive reflexes, together with postural reactions that fail to develop, are the hallmark of an upper motor neuron abnormality in an infant ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/introduction.html)). Examining the two together is a simple, quick and predictive screen for infants at risk of cerebral palsy ([Zafeiriou 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15246484/)).

**Why they come and go**

The primitive reflexes are generated low in the nervous system and are present at birth. As the cortex and its descending pathways mature, they suppress these reflexes, and when descending control is damaged the reflex persists. The postural reactions depend on the same maturing control, so the same damage leaves them late or absent, and one lesion produces two signs pointing the same way.

**Use the slider in the figure above** to move from birth to 12 months. The ages come from the Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam.

- Rooting disappears at about 4 months and the Moro by 4 to 5 months, so a Moro or asymmetric tonic neck reflex still present at 6 months is abnormal.
- The Landau should develop by 4 to 5 months and lateral propping by 5 to 7 months, and the parachute usually appears at 8 to 9 months. A parachute that is absent at 12 months or asymmetric at any age is abnormal.
- An upgoing toe is normal through the first year, and hand preference before 12 months is a red flag.

**Asymmetric reflexes**

A symmetric delay suggests a global problem, and an **asymmetric** reflex is a localizing sign. A parachute that extends only one arm, or a grasp that persists in one hand, usually points to the motor pathway of the opposite hemisphere, though a brachial plexus injury on the same side can look similar. An absent plantar grasp in the first 6 months correlates with poor neurologic development (DeMyer, p. 282). Short videos of each reflex are on the Utah site at [3 months](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/03month.html), [6 months](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/06month.html) and [12 months](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/12month.html).
keyPoints: Primitive reflexes such as the Moro, grasp and Galant fade over 4 to 6 months, and postural reactions emerge from about 3 to 8 months (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Persistent primitive reflexes with absent postural reactions are an upper motor neuron sign in infancy (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
A Moro or asymmetric tonic neck reflex at 6 months is abnormal, and the parachute should be present by 12 months.
Asymmetry localizes, so a one-sided parachute or a grasp persisting in one hand usually points to the opposite hemisphere, although a brachial plexus injury can look the same.
Examined together, primitive reflexes and postural reactions are a quick screen for infants at risk of cerebral palsy (Zafeiriou 2004).

question.question: At 7 months, an infant born at 35 weeks still has a full Moro response and a persistent asymmetric tonic neck reflex, and does not prop sideways when tipped. Tone in the legs feels increased. How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Normal for a preterm infant; reassess at 18 months
A sign of a peripheral nerve or muscle disorder
An isolated vestibular problem, because the Moro is a vestibular reflex
Possible upper motor neuron dysfunction, such as evolving cerebral palsy, warranting a careful examination and referral
question.explanation: Persistent primitive reflexes with absent postural reactions are the hallmark of an upper motor neuron abnormality in an infant, and a Moro or asymmetric tonic neck reflex at 6 months is abnormal (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). Even corrected for prematurity, this infant is past 6 months, and with increased leg tone the pattern suggests evolving cerebral palsy. Nerve and muscle disease would not do this.

sections.title: Reading each finding against age
sections.content:
Stroke a newborn's palm and her fingers close round yours, which is exactly what they should do. Draw the same grip from an adult whose frontal lobes are failing and it means something else entirely. Across a lifetime the palmar grasp goes from present and normal, to absent and normal, to present again and abnormal. In the newborn the grasp shows that the lower parts of the motor system work. Its fading shows descending control arriving, and its return shows that control failing.

A lesion's place in the nervous system needs three spatial coordinates, and in a child it needs a fourth, **time since birth**. In an adult an upgoing toe is an upper motor neuron sign whenever you find it. In a child the same observation can be a normal stage, a warning, or a leftover from infancy. The basic unit of the pediatric exam is the pair **(finding, age)**. The first standard of abnormality is comparison with the norm for the patient's age (DeMyer, p. 36), and in a child that comparison is half the work.

**Findings whose meaning depends on age**

- An **upgoing toe** is normal in the first year, while myelination is incomplete, and later it is an upper motor neuron sign ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)).
- **Hand preference** is ordinary in a schoolchild and abnormal before 12 months, when it points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/06month.html)).
- The **primitive reflexes** should fade on schedule. Their persistence, with postural reactions that fail to arrive, is an upper motor neuron sign in an infant ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/introduction.html)) and an early marker of cerebral palsy ([Zafeiriou 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15246484/)).
- The grasp, suck and rooting responses can **return** later in life when frontal control fails, as frontal release signs (Pearl 2014, p. 114).

**Reactions that fail to appear**

A postural reaction that should have arrived and hasn't is as informative as a reflex that should have gone and hasn't ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/introduction.html)). A Moro still present at 6 months and an upgoing toe at 6 years say the same thing, that the descending motor pathway is not doing its job. Age only moves the line where normal ends. When [[m03-first-fork|Module 3]] asks whether a weakness is upper or lower motor neuron, part of an infant's answer comes from reflexes that failed to disappear, so record the age beside every finding.
keyPoints: In a child, localization has a fourth coordinate, time since birth, so a sign is really a pair of finding and age.
An upgoing toe is normal in the first year, and hand preference before 12 months is abnormal (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Primitive reflexes should fade on schedule, and their persistence is an upper motor neuron sign in infancy (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam; Zafeiriou 2004).
The same reflexes can return later in life as frontal release signs (Pearl 2014, p. 114).
Age does not change what a sign says about the circuit, but it moves the line where normal ends.

question.question: Two children grip your fingers firmly and will not let go when you stroke their palms. One is a 2-week-old who is feeding well. The other is a 12-year-old who has become apathetic and disinhibited over three months and cannot stop grasping even when asked not to hold on. How should the grasp be read in each?
options: Normal in both, because the grasp is a normal human reflex
Abnormal in both, because a grasp reflex always means frontal lobe disease
Normal in the newborn; in the 12-year-old a release sign pointing to the frontal lobes, which needs investigation
Abnormal in the newborn, who should have lost it before birth; normal in the 12-year-old
question.explanation: The palmar grasp is expected in a newborn and fades over the first months (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). In a 12-year-old, a grasp the child cannot suppress on request is a frontal release sign, an infant reflex returning because frontal control has failed (Pearl 2014, p. 114), and with a change in behavior it needs investigation. Only the pair of finding and age carries meaning.

quiz.question: A resident examining an alert, cooperative 10-year-old with migraine performs a full examination including smell, taste, two-point discrimination and calorics. What principle does this violate?
options: Expect the abnormal
Screen everyone, then expand or trim the examination to fit the history
Compare with the family
Undress the patient
quiz.explanation: A brief screening examination should be expanded or trimmed to fit the history (DeMyer, p. 604; Morris 2012, p. xxv). A child with a typical migraine history needs a careful screen and a look at the optic discs, and smell, taste, two-point discrimination and calorics add nothing. 'Expect the abnormal' is about vigilance, not about doing more tests.

quiz.question: Which of these is the best way to record a normal motor examination in a 5-year-old?
options: Motor: WNL
Motor: non-focal
Walks, runs and hops on each foot; rises from the floor without using hands; strength full in arms and legs; tone normal; reflexes 2+ and symmetric; toes down
Motor: 5/5 throughout
quiz.explanation: The record should show what was tested and what was found, so the next reader can check it (DeMyer, pp. 36, 604). The descriptive note covers gait, functional strength, tone, reflexes and plantar responses in a few words. 'WNL' and 'non-focal' are conclusions without evidence, and '5/5 throughout' reports strength alone in a child better judged by what they can do.

quiz.question: You want to test hip and leg strength in a 3-year-old who will not cooperate with formal testing. Which approach gives the most reliable information?
options: Ask him to push against your hand with each leg
Test strength under sedation
Rely on the parents' description of his running
Watch him rise from sitting on the floor, climb onto a chair and run to fetch a ball
quiz.explanation: Rising from the floor, climbing and running show proximal leg strength without asking for cooperation, and running to fetch something is a quick screen of gait (Brazis 2011, p. 17). Formal resistance testing in an uncooperative 3-year-old is unreliable, sedation removes the movement you want to see, and the parents' account is history rather than examination.

quiz.question: A 4-month-old held in prone suspension lifts her head but not yet her legs, still shows a Moro, and has a strong palmar grasp. How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Consistent with normal development at 4 months
Abnormal, because the Moro should be gone by now
Abnormal, because the Landau should be complete
Abnormal, because the palmar grasp should be absent
quiz.explanation: At 4 months the Moro and the grasp are still fading, since they diminish over 4 to 6 months, and the Landau is expected by 4 to 5 months, so a partial Landau is within range (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). A Moro becomes abnormal if it is still present at 6 months. The pattern is age-appropriate, and re-examination later would confirm the expected changes.

quiz.question: At 10 months, a baby tipped forward toward the mat extends the right arm but keeps the left arm flexed against the body. What does this suggest?
options: Normal, because the parachute is not expected until 12 months
Weakness of the left arm, pointing to the right hemisphere or the left brachial plexus, needing a full examination
Weakness of the right arm
A visual problem
quiz.explanation: The parachute usually appears at 8 to 9 months, and an asymmetric parachute suggests weakness of the arm that fails to extend (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). The rest of the examination decides between the right hemisphere, with brisk reflexes and increased tone, and the left brachial plexus, with reduced tone and reflexes. Waiting for 12 months ignores the asymmetry.

signOff: Performs a complete neurologic examination on a toddler, in a developmentally appropriate order, observed by faculty.

opener.parable: Anyone who has tried to test a two-year-old's visual fields knows how quickly a planned examination can fall apart. The child looks at you, at the toy, at the door, and the careful sequence you had in mind is gone. The examination works only when each step is a small experiment the child is willing to take part in.
opener.history: Harvey Cushing (1869–1939) wrote that the instruments of precision multiplying around him were "as nothing compared with" the careful study of the patient by a keen observer using eyes, ears and fingers.
